pr_title: Add support for IRQ vector tables with jump opcodes and direct ISRs on RISCV
pr_body:
Fixes: #46799

The whole mechanism of IRQ table generation is built around the assumption that the IRQ vector table contains an array of addresses the PC will be assigned to when the corresponding interrupt is triggered. For example:
```
#define ISR_WRAPPER ((uintptr_t)&_isr_wrapper)

uintptr_t __irq_vector_table _irq_vector_table[64] = {
   ISR_WRAPPER,
   ISR_WRAPPER,
   ...
};
```
While this is correct for the majority of architectures (ARM, RISCV with CLIC in vectored mode, etc...) this is not valid in general (for example RISCV with CLINT/HLINT in vectored mode).
    
In this alternative format for the IRQ vector table, the pc will get assigned by the hardware to the address of the vector table index corresponding to the interrupt ID. From the vector table index, a subsequent jump will occur from there to service the interrupt.
    
This means that the IRQ vector table contains an opcode that is a jump instruction to a specific location instead of the address of the location itself. For example:

```
SECTION_FUNC(vectors, _irq_vector_table)
   .option norvc
   j _isr_wrapper
   j _isr_wrapper
   ...
```
    
This patchset is introducing support for this alternative IRQ vector table format. The user can now select one format or the other one by acting on `IRQ_VECTOR_TABLE_JUMP_BY_ADDRESS` or `IRQ_VECTOR_TABLE_JUMP_BY_CODE` Kconfig symbols.

Leveraging the work on the IRQ vector table this patchset is also adding support for direct ISRs on RISCV.

issue_context.title: IRQ vector table: how to support different formats
issue_context.body:
Right now the only architecture actually using the IRQ vector table generation is ARM (and X86?). The whole mechanism of table generation is build around the assumption that the table has a format compatible with a generic ARM vector table: that is an array of function pointers saved as `uintptr_t`. For example:
```
#define ISR_WRAPPER ((uintptr_t)&_isr_wrapper)

uintptr_t __irq_vector_table _irq_vector_table[64] = {
   ISR_WRAPPER,
   ISR_WRAPPER,
   ...
};
```
Unfortunately this is not always the case. For RISCV, for example, the IRQ vector table contains not just the address of the destination function to jump to, but an actual assembly instruction. For example (in assembly):
```
SECTION_FUNC(vectors, _irq_vector_table)
   .option norvc
   j _isr_wrapper
   j _isr_wrapper
   ...
```
Now, the IRQ vector table as generated by Zephyr is always a C file containing the `uintptr_t` array, so it is not easy to adapt that to the format expected for RISCV.

How we should modify this mechanism to be as generic as possible?

1. Modify the `arch/common/gen_isr_tables.py` script to generate a different kind of table according to an external parameter.
2. Having a different `gen_isr_tables.py` script for each arch
3. Switch to something else entirely.
4. ???
comments: Option 1 seems like a good idea since you only need a different output by adding a new output function. The code to extract interrupts from the binary image should be the same for all architectures..... unless this is not the case here.

Unless I'm mistaken, the RISC-V table is meant to allow different entry
points for different exception causes. This is not the same as having
different IRQ vectors.

Uhm, according to [0], when in vectored mode:
```
The interrupt handler offset is calculated by mtvec.base + (mcause.code * 4). For example,
software interrupts with ID of 3 would trap to offset mtvec.base + 0xC. The first entry in the
table supports exceptions since they trap to the base address defined in mtvec. There is no
vector table for exception handling.
```

So my understanding is that all the exceptions are going to use the first entry of the IRQ vector table. As long as you do not install a direct ISR in the first entry, this entry will always be containing a jump to `_isr_wrapper` that should take care of handling the various exceptions.

Am I getting this wrong @npitre ?

[0] https://starfivetech.com/uploads/sifive-interrupt-cookbook-v1p2.pdf

mcause is not related to IRQ numbers. It is about "Instruction address 
misaligned", "Instruction Access fault", "Illegal instruction", "Load 
access fault", etc.

> mcause is not related to IRQ numbers. It is about "Instruction address
misaligned", "Instruction Access fault", "Illegal instruction", "Load
access fault", etc.

AFAICT `mcause` is also about interrupts. In the spec we have `The Interrupt bit in the mcause register is set if the trap was caused by an interrupt. The Exception Code field contains a code identifying the last exception or interrupt`. So when in vectored mode, you are going to set PC to `mtvec.base + (mcause.code * 4)`.

Now, for CLINT / HLINT you can read the interrupt number directly from `mcause` (for example `Exception Code 7 == Machine timer interrupt`), for PLIC all the IRQs are going to trigger the Exception Code 11 and then you can actually retrieve the IRQ number from the PLIC.

> AFAICT `mcause` is also about interrupts. In the spec we have `The 
> Interrupt bit in the mcause register is set if the trap was caused 
> by an interrupt.

Agreed. Although not all implementations support that bit, apparently.

> The Exception Code field contains a code identifying the last exception
> or interrupt`. So when in vectored mode, you are going to set PC to 
> `mtvec.base + (mcause.code * 4)`.

Well OK.

You still have to do all the register context save, the stack switch, etc.
for each IRQ vector.

Right now there is nothing duplicating that code for each of them.

> Agreed. Although not all implementations support that bit, apparently.

Interesting. I need to look into this.

> You still have to do all the register context save, the stack switch, etc. for each IRQ vector.
> 
> Right now there is nothing duplicating that code for each of them.

The IRQ vector table as proposed in #46980 works this way: when you don't have a direct ISR installed (that is a special kind of ISR) by default all the table entries are redirected to the old `_isr_wrapper`, so you have all the old code as usual and everything should be exactly as before.

When you install a direct ISR you don't jump to `_isr_wrapper` but you jump to a special (very quick) ISR. This ISR is marked as `__((interrupt))__` so the compiler should take care of the context saving for you and in general the things you can do from inside a direct ISR are very limited.
